contentBeforeToc:
Checkout.liquid is not new, and not as famous as it once was. Henceforth, Shopify has replaced custom checkout code with Checkout Extensibility, a structured, supported framework built around specific tools rather than open template editing.

If your last checkout project predates this shift, the rules have genuinely changed. Here’s what you can actually customize now through Shopify checkout customization, and where the real limits sit.
contentAfterToc:
The Four Building Blocks

Checkout Extensibility isn’t one feature; it’s four separate tools, each owning a different slice of the checkout experience:

  • Checkout UI Extensions: Structured components that render in specific checkout slots, banners, custom fields, content blocks, upsell offers.
  • Shopify Functions: Backend logic for discounts, shipping rules, and payment customization, replacing the older Shopify Scripts.
  • Checkout Branding API: Styling control, colors, fonts, logo, layout, without touching functional logic.
  • Web Pixels: Event tracking for conversions, replacing the old “Additional Scripts” approach to analytics.

What You Can Customize on Standard Plans

Standard and Advanced plans give you real, if more limited, control: checkout branding (logo, colors, fonts) and basic form field toggles through the built-in checkout editor. This covers visual consistency and simple field adjustments without needing custom development.

What Requires Shopify Plus

Deeper customization, custom content blocks, upsell offers, and Functions-driven logic like custom discount or shipping rules are where Plus pulls ahead significantly. This is one of the clearest remaining reasons brands upgrade specifically for checkout control.

What You Can’t Do, Regardless of Plan

Some things are simply off the table. Your theme doesn’t control checkout at all; it’s a separate, Shopify-hosted surface. Once a shopper clicks “Checkout,” Shopify takes over rendering entirely, which is also why switching themes never breaks your checkout.

Custom code no longer lives directly in a checkout template; it runs in sandboxed extensions instead. That’s a deliberate trade-off: more limited than the old open-editing model, but far more stable and secure.

Deadlines That Actually Matter Right Now

  • June 30, 2026: Shopify Scripts (used for discount, shipping, and payment logic) stop working entirely. Anything still running on Scripts needs to migrate to Shopify Functions.
  • August 26, 2026: Non-Plus stores must upgrade their Thank You and Order Status pages. Additional Scripts and script tags on these pages stop working, and any tracking built that way needs to move to Web Pixels.

If you’re still relying on old Additional Scripts for tracking or checkout logic, the safest move is to start the migration now; developer availability narrows fast as deadlines approach, and the actual work doesn’t get easier by waiting.

When Custom Development Is Actually Required

Most checkout needs — branding, basic fields, standard upsells — are now covered by Extensibility’s supported tools directly, or by apps built on top of them. Custom development becomes genuinely necessary when your business needs Functions-based logic specific to your operation: complex discount stacking, non-standard shipping calculations, or checkout behavior tied to unique business rules no off-the-shelf app already handles.

A Common Misconception

“Extensibility means I can’t customize checkout” isn’t accurate. You can customize a great deal; it just happens through structured APIs now instead of open template editing. Most modern checkout apps are themselves built on these same Extensibility tools; installing one is often faster than building custom, unless your logic is genuinely unique.

The Bottom Line

Checkout customization on Shopify today is more structured, and more secure, than it used to be. Know which of the four building blocks your need actually falls into, and you’ll know quickly whether it’s covered by native tools, an existing app, or genuinely requires custom development.
